paper_title: SWE-Trail: History-Guided Trajectory Collection for Coding Agent Training

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Coding agents solve repository issues through long sequences of exploration, editing, and validation. These trajectories are increasingly used as post-training data, so how they are collected shapes what the trained model learns. A common approach is to sample multiple trajectories independently for each issue and then select or curate them. However, as more trajectories are sampled independently, later trajectories become increasingly redundant, even though earlier trajectories could guide where subsequent collection effort should be spent. A natural way to use this history is to expose it to the coding agent as advice. But training on such trajectories can make the model rely on advice that is unavailable at test time, creating a train-test mismatch. Instead, we argue that history should guide where collection effort is spent, while the coding agent decides what to generate. We introduce SWE-Trail, a trajectory collector that uses earlier trajectories to guide subsequent collection while keeping that history outside the coding agent's context. During a new rollout, SWE-Trail uses history to identify a state where additional collection effort may be useful. There, the coding agent proposes candidate next actions from its ordinary context, and SWE-Trail briefly executes them from the same checkpoint to decide which route continues. We evaluate collection approaches by training student models on the trajectories they produce. For a 124B student initialized from Ling-3.0-flash-base, SWE-Trail improves mean resolution over independent sampling by 2.33 and 1.60 percentage points on SWE-bench Multilingual and SWE-bench Pro, respectively. Without history, the same pipeline produces more resolved trajectories than independent sampling, but improves by only 0.11 points on Multilingual. These results show the value of using history to guide collection without exposing it to the coding agent.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Resolving repository-level issue requires coding agent to explore the repository, modify code, and validate its changes (Jimenez et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2024). These interactions form trajectories that record not only the final patch but also the agents reasoning and actions throughout the repair process. Such trajectories are increasingly used as post-training data, so the collection process directly affects their value for training (Chen et al., 2026; Han, 2026). common way to collect coding agent training trajectories is to sample several trajectories per issue and keep those that pass tests or judge (Ehrlich et al., 2025; Jain et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2025). Some work also edits the kept trajectories, masking flawed tool calls or removing redundant steps (Han et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026a; Tao et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026b). These methods operate after trajectories are collected, while trajectories for the same issue are still generated independently. However, later independent samples become increasingly redundant as more trajectories are collected. They often revisit repair targets and behaviors already explored earlier. Rather than ignoring this history, subsequent collection can use earlier trajectories to decide where additional collection effort should be spent. For example, disagreements between successful and failed trajectories can reveal decision points where alternative actions are worth comparing. We refer to such evidence as allocation signals and to the earlier trajectories for an issue as its history. Section 2 quantifies the redundancy of independent sampling and tests whether earlier trajectories provide such allocation 1 SWE-Trail signals. Since earlier trajectories can provide useful information for new rollout, natural way to use this history is to place it in the coding agents context as advice (Chen et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b). This can help the current rollout, but the resulting training trajectories record reasoning and actions generated with access to the advice. However, at test time, the trained model must make decisions without that advice. As result, these trajectories may provide less useful supervision for training, as we evaluate in Section 4.2. This leads to our central question: How can history guide where collection effort is spent while the coding agent decides what to generate from its ordinary context? To answer this question, we introduce SWE-Trail, trajectory collector that keeps history outside the coding agents context. Before collection, SWE-Trail uses history to determine which states should receive more collection effort and what evidence should be considered at those states. During new rollout, when the agent reaches such state, it proposes candidate next actions from its ordinary context without access to the history. SWE-Trail then compares candidate actions by briefly executing them from the same checkpoint. It selects the route that is better supported by repository evidence. The coding agent then continues from the selected route to complete the trajectory. concrete example illustrates this process. On Rust issue, all prior failed trajectories made an edit and then continued reading without running tests. From this history, SWE-Trail determines that this state should receive additional collection effort when it appears again in new rollout. When the rollout reaches such state, the coding agent proposes different next actions from its ordinary context, including further reading and running tests. SWE-Trail briefly executes both choices from the same checkpoint and selects the test-running route based on the resulting evidence. The coding agent then continues from the selected route until the rollout ends. We evaluate whether SWE-Trail collects trajectories that are more useful for downstream training. The comparison uses the same 300 SWE-rebench V2 issues (Badertdinov et al., 2026). Each setting collects five trajectories per issue with GLM-5.1 (GLM-5 Team, 2026; Z.ai, 2026). SeedBank provides the independent sampling baseline. H5 uses the five SeedBank trajectories for each issue as history to collect five new trajectories, while H0 runs the same collection pipeline without history. We train the 124B Ling-3.0-flash-base model (inclusionAI, 2026) on the trajectories from each condition, with three independent training runs. Under this controlled setup, H5 improves mean resolution over SeedBank by 2.33 and 1.60 percentage points on SWE-bench Multilingual and SWE-bench Pro, respectively. The H0 control helps isolate the contribution of history. It produces more resolved trajectories than SeedBank, but improves the 124B students mean resolution by only 0.11 points on Multilingual. This contrast shows that collection success alone does not explain the downstream gain. second student model, Qwen3-14B-Base (Qwen Team, 2025), is also trained on the same H5 trajectories to test whether the gain generalizes across student models. For Qwen3-14B-Base, H5 improves mean resolution over SeedBank by 3.11 and 2.42 percentage points on SWE-bench Multilingual and SWE-bench Pro, respectively. Together, these results support using history to guide trajectory collection without placing that history in the coding agents context.

sections.title: 2 Motivation
sections.content: To examine the empirical basis for our motivation, we analyze the independently sampled trajectories in SeedBank. We use attempt to refer to one independent try at solving an issue, and examine both how coverage grows with additional attempts and whether earlier attempts provide allocation signals for subsequent collection.

sections.title: 2.1 Diminishing Coverage Gains from Independent Rollouts
sections.content: Figure 1A shows the expected number of issues solved with attempts per issue, averaging over all k-attempt subsets of the five SeedBank attempts for each issue. For given k-attempt subset, an issue is counted as solved if at least one of the attempts succeeds. With one attempt per issue, 58.4 issues are solved in expectation. Increasing from 1 to 2 adds 13.1 solved issues, while increasing it to 3, 4, and 5 adds only 8.0, 5.1, and 3.4 more issues, respectively. Thus, each additional attempt still expands issue coverage, but by smaller amount. 2 SWE-Trail Figure 1. Diminishing coverage gains from independent rollouts. A: expected number of issues solved with attempts per issue. Gray labels show marginal additions. B: mean coverage of each issues five-attempt patch-target union, grouped by SeedBank outcomes. Both panels average over all k-attempt subsets of the five recorded attempts. The vertical axis in starts at 65%. Patch-target coverage shows the same diminishing pattern across different types of history. We use modified files as patch targets and define three history types from each issues SeedBank outcomes: stablesolved if all attempts succeed, mixed if both successful and failed attempts occur, and never-solved if all attempts fail. For each history type, Figure 1B shows the fraction of files modified across an issues five attempts that are covered by attempts. We average this fraction over all k-attempt subsets and then across issues. One attempt already covers 90.0% of these files on stable-solved issues, 73.2% on mixed issues, and 80.1% on never-solved issues. These results show substantial target overlap across all three history types. As more attempts are added, later attempts cover fewer new files. Overlap among successful attempts may simply reflect convergence on the same repair targets. However, even when all independent attempts fail, they still modify many of the same files. This pattern shows that independent sampling does not automatically redirect collection effort after repeated failures. Later attempts may continue spending effort on previously explored repair targets rather than exploring new ones. Together with the issue-level results, these findings show that later independent attempts become increasingly redundant.

sections.title: 2.2 History Provides Allocation Signals
sections.content: Section 2.1 shows that later independent attempts add less coverage and often revisit repair targets explored earlier. The remaining question is whether history can indicate where additional collection effort may be useful. Mixed issues are informative because successful and failed attempts may choose different next actions from similar states. We therefore examine whether such decision points occur. For each mixed issue, an auditor compares the most similar successful and failed attempts and locates their first meaningful decision difference. We assess whether the two attempts are similar enough to compare their next actions and whether both actions are reasonable at that point. The audit is conducted independently with GPT-5.6-Sol (OpenAI, 2026) and GLM-5.1. The main analysis includes 43 of the 51 mixed issues, excluding eight whose failed attempt ended in timeout or collector error. GPT-5.6-Sol identifies such cases in 26 issues and GLM-5.1 in 31, with 20 identified by both models. These results show that mixed histories can reveal decision points where additional collection effort may be useful. The detailed results are reported in Appendix A.3. However, this evidence relies on having both successful and failed attempts. To test whether history remains useful without one, we examine never-solved histories and measure the overlap in modified files across failed attempts on the same issue. The mean pairwise Jaccard overlap is 0.841. Among the 198 issues with defined overlap score, 93 have score of 1.0. These results show that failed attempts often focus on the same repair targets. This overlap does not explain why the attempts fail, but it shows where effort is repeatedly spent across failed attempts. Thus, even without successfailure contrast, history can still indicate where additional collection effort may be useful. Together, these findings show that history can provide allocation signals for collection. Appendix gives the audit procedure and overlap calculations. 3 SWE-Trail Figure 2. SWE-Trail in two stages. Offline, the compiler reads the issue history, runs bounded read-only repository checks, and freezes an acquisition record Ri containing detector Di, comparison objective ui, and sampling schedule λi. Online, when Di identifies state for additional collection effort, the coding agent proposes candidate next actions from its ordinary context. SWE-Trail briefly executes two candidates from the same checkpoint, and an identity-blind selector retains the route better supported by repository evidence under ui. The coding agent then continues from the selected route. History never enters the coding agents context.

sections.title: 3 SWE-Trail
sections.content: Section 2 shows that later independent attempts add less new coverage, while earlier attempts can indicate where additional collection effort may be useful. Motivated by these observations, we introduce SWE-Trail, trajectory collector that uses history to decide where additional collection effort should be spent in new rollout. For issue i, let xi contain the issue statement and the repository snapshot at the issue commit. The history Hi contains the attempts already collected on that issue. SWE-Trail has access to Hi, but the coding agent does not. Reference patches are unavailable during collection. Figure 2 shows the two stages of SWE-Trail. Before collection, SWE-Trail uses the history and read-only repository checks to determine which states should receive additional collection effort and what evidence should be considered at those states. During rollout, when such state is reached, the coding agent proposes candidate next actions from its ordinary context without access to the history. SWE-Trail selects candidates for comparison, briefly executes them in parallel from the same checkpoint, and retains the route better supported by repository evidence. The coding agent then continues from the selected route to complete the trajectory.

sections.title: 3.1 Compiling History into Detectors
sections.content: Earlier attempts can indicate which states should receive additional collection effort, but new rollout may reach similar situations through different sequence of actions. The compiler therefore builds detector Di whose rules recognize such states from the rollouts actions and observations rather than relying on fixed step numbers. For example, the detector in Figure 2 recognizes repeated reading after an edit without validation. The runtime checks these rules after each new repository observation and samples candidate actions when state matches. 4 SWE-Trail To build the detector, the compiler first analyzes (xi, Hi) to extract allocation signals from the history. These signals include decisions supported by successful attempts, differences across repair routes, and recurring failures. The history may leave open questions about the issue or repository, so the compiler then runs bounded read-only repository checks to resolve these questions. These checks do not modify source code or access the reference patch. The compiler stores the historical evidence, check results, and remaining questions in private acquisition record Ri. Using Ri, the compiler defines the detector rules and local comparison objective ui(d) for each detector state d. The objective specifies what evidence should be considered when comparing candidate routes at that state. Different histories lead the compiler to focus on different kinds of decisions. For stable-solved histories, repeated success shows which decisions already have strong support. The compiler allocates additional effort only when meaningful uncertainty remains. For mixed histories, it focuses on states where successful and failed repair routes differ. For never-solved histories, it focuses on recurring failure patterns, such as edits followed by further reading without validation. The compiler also sets sampling-temperature schedule λi for candidate generation when detector state is reached. Mixed and never-solved histories use higher temperatures to encourage more varied next actions when the history shows unresolved choices or repeated failures. Before collection begins, the compiler validates each proposed detector state against its supporting evidence and replays its rules on the recorded attempts. States without sufficient support are discarded. The admitted detector states, their comparison objectives, and λi are then fixed for the entire collection round. Appendices and F.5 provide the compiler details, admission checks, and example records.

sections.title: 3.2 Sampling Comparable Alternatives
sections.content: The detector determines where additional collection effort is spent, while the actions to consider come from the coding agent itself. When the rollout reaches state recognized by Di, SWE-Trail samples several candidate next actions using only the agents ordinary context. The history, acquisition record Ri, and comparison objective ui(d) are not added to that context. The first sample uses the agents ordinary temperature and serves as the default. The remaining samples use λi. Different samples may propose equivalent actions, so SWE-Trail first groups equivalent proposals together. It keeps the default candidate and shortlists executable alternatives from the remaining proposals. To keep each intervention local and bounded, SWE-Trail chooses at most one alternative from this shortlist using Ri and ui(d). If no suitable alternative is available, the rollout continues with the default action. Otherwise, SWE-Trail restores two isolated workspaces from the same checkpoint, one for the default and one for the chosen alternative. Both candidates start from the same conversation and workspace state and run for the same short horizon, producing two executed suffixes of actions and observations. To avoid expanding collection into multi-level search tree, each trajectory performs at most one such comparison. Different rollouts on the same issue may still make their comparison at different detector states.

sections.title: 3.3 Selecting a Route by Executed Evidence
sections.content: Once both suffixes have been executed, SWE-Trail compares their progress using the local comparison objective ui(d). The two suffixes are presented to SWE-Trail in shuffled order, hiding which one comes from the default candidate. SWE-Trail uses Ri only as background for the comparison. It prefers route only when the two executed suffixes provide clear evidence that one makes better progress under ui(d). Otherwise, it keeps the default. After selection, the coding agent continues only from the selected workspace until the full rollout ends. For training, SWE-Trail keeps only the selected route, preserves the coding agents original reasoning and actions without rewriting, and removes the unselected suffix and private collector events. This ensures that the training record remains single continuous trajectory generated by the coding agent and that private collection information does not enter the training process. Algorithm 1 in Appendix summarizes the procedure, and Appendix H.1 provides full end-to-end case study. 5 Table 1. H5 improves downstream resolution on both benchmarks. sections.title: 4.1 Setting
sections.content: We test whether training on SWE-Trail trajectories improves student performance on new issues. Across all comparisons, we use the same collection issues and the same number of coding trajectories for training. The background training data and the training and evaluation protocols remain fixed. Shared setting. Each training dataset contains five coding trajectories for each of the same 300 SWErebench V2 issues (Badertdinov et al., 2026), giving 1,500 trajectories in total. None of the collection repositories appears in either evaluation benchmark. All coding rollouts use GLM-5.1 (GLM-5 Team, 2026) with the OpenHands scaffold (Wang et al., 2025a). Collection runs in an offline sandbox with repository commit histories removed. Reference patches and published fixes are unavailable during collection. Appendix details the provenance of the collection issues and verifies that they share no issues or repositories with either evaluation benchmark. Methods and variants. SeedBank provides the independent-sampling baseline. We apply controlled adaptations of SWE-Gym (Pan et al., 2025), SWE-TRACE (Han et al., 2026), and SWE-Lego (Tao et al., 2026) to the same SeedBank trajectories. We also adapt SWE-Exp (Chen et al., 2025) to test different use of history, where the coding agent reads an experience message compiled from the SeedBank attempts during collection. The message is retained in the training record. For SWE-Trail, history remains outside the coding agents context throughout collection. Its main variant, H5, uses the five SeedBank attempts for each issue as history when collecting five new trajectories. H0 sets Hi = and runs the same read-only repository checks and compiler without history. Comparing H0 with SeedBank tests the collection pipeline without history, while comparing H5 with H0 isolates what history adds. We also use two H5 variants to test where SWE-Trail makes comparisons and which route it retains. Random detection replaces the history-guided comparison location with random eligible state while keeping H5s remaining collection procedure unchanged. Random retention keeps H5s detector but randomly chooses which executed route to continue. Both variants use the same per-trajectory model-call limits and execution horizon as H5. To examine history scale, H10 adds five independently sampled attempts to the five attempts already used by H5 for each issue. It otherwise uses the same read-only repository checks and compiler, so comparing H10 with H5 tests whether more history adds value. We also compare SWE-Trail with verifier-based trajectory selection. Top-5-of-10 selects five of ten independently sampled trajectories per issue. Top-5-hybrid applies the same verifier to five SeedBank and five H5 trajectories and selects five from the combined set. Table 13 in Appendix gives the full experimental conditions. Appendices B.5 and B.6 provide the runtime settings and export checks. Table 2. H10 costs 12.9% more recorded tokens than H5 for 0.22/0.14 point gain. Differences are relative to H0. Acquisition-only tokens exclude the ordinary rollout and total tokens include it. : H0 omits offline compiler calls, so its compute is lower bound and the differences are upper bounds.

sections.title: 4.2 Downstream Training Utility
sections.content: SWE-Trail improves downstream resolution. Table 1 shows that H5 outperforms all other conditions in the table on both benchmarks. H5 improves mean resolution over SeedBank by 2.33 percentage points on Multilingual and 1.60 points on SWE-Pro. Since the dataset size and training setup are fixed, these differences reflect changes in the collected trajectories. Across three independent training runs, every H5 run exceeds every SeedBank run on both benchmarks. An exact one-sided permutation test over the training runs gives = 0.05 on each benchmark. Appendix reports the individual runs, statistical tests, and results by language. SWE-Exp falls below SeedBank by 1.33 points on Multilingual and 2.78 points on SWE-Pro. This may reflect reliance on advice available during training but absent at evaluation. To examine the role of advice more directly, Appendix H.2 compares two exports of the same trajectories, with the advice either retained or removed. Compared with retaining the advice, removing it improves SWE-Pro but lowers Multilingual. Removing the advice after collection does not remove its influence on how the trajectory was generated. The agent produced its reasoning after reading the advice, so some decisions may remain without the information that originally supported them. H5 has higher mean resolution than H0. Without history, H0 improves mean resolution over SeedBank by 0.11 points on Multilingual and 0.73 points on SWE-Pro. Adding history in H5 raises mean resolution by further 2.22 and 0.87 points over H0, respectively. The point estimates are positive on both benchmarks, but task-paired bootstrap gives 95% intervals of [0.2, 4.6] points on Multilingual and [0.8, 2.5] on SWE-Pro. Appendix E.2 gives the full paired analysis. Section 4.4 compares these downstream differences with the corresponding collection outcomes. Both collection decisions matter. To test these two choices, we randomize each one separately. Random detection replaces H5s history-guided choice of where to compare with random eligible point and lowers mean resolution by 1.44 points on Multilingual and 1.28 points on SWE-Pro. Random retention keeps H5s history-guided comparison location but randomly chooses which executed route continues, lowering mean resolution by 0.89 and 1.19 points, respectively. These decreases support using history to decide where additional collection effort should be spent and execution evidence to decide which route should continue. Both variants remain above SeedBank in mean resolution, while their run ranges overlap H5s on both benchmarks. The gains extend to another student. We repeat the comparison with Qwen3-14B-Base using the same SeedBank, H0, and H5 trajectory sets. H5 improves mean resolution over SeedBank by 3.11 percentage points on Multilingual and 2.42 points on SWE-Pro. It also exceeds H0 by 1.67 and 1.60 points, respectively. These results show that the downstream gains from SWE-Trail also appear with another student model. 7 SWE-Trail Appendix E.4 gives the full results.

sections.title: 4.3 History Scale and Cost
sections.content: More history brings smaller gains. Table 2 compares H0, H5, and H10. Using five prior attempts improves mean resolution over H0 by 2.22 points on Multilingual and 0.87 points on SWE-Pro. Increasing the history from five to ten attempts adds only 0.22 and 0.14 points, respectively. H10 also does not improve the collection outcomes over H5, despite increasing tokens spent beyond the ordinary rollout from 307M to 510M, 66.0% increase, and total collection tokens by 12.9%. More history therefore provides only small additional mean gains at substantially higher collection overhead. The main H5 setting remains close to H0 in cost. Excluding the cost of collecting prior attempts, H5 uses at most 3.7% more tokens than H0. Its ordinary rollouts use 4.4% fewer tokens than H0. The same diminishing gain appears with Qwen3-14B-Base. sections.content: Collection success does not explain student gains. Table 4 compares the collection outcomes. Relative to SeedBank, H0 produces 37 more resolved trajectories, but improves the student by only 0.11 points on Multilingual. Adding history in H5 produces 16 more resolved trajectories and solves six more issues than H0, while improving the student by further 2.22 points. Across both benchmarks, the downstream gain is not proportional to the increase in resolved trajectories. Table 4. Collection outcomes over 1,500 trajectories per method. We examine how H5 and H0 trajectories differ beyond their final outcomes using the process statistics in Table 19 of Appendix F. Relative to H0, H5 reduces the mean number of actions from 40.89 to 39.51 and repeated file reads from 7.59 to 7.01. The share of edited trajectories with check after the final edit increases slightly from 88.91% to 89.53%. The clearest shift is toward shorter repair processes with fewer repeated reads, while post-final-edit checking changes only slightly. Appendix F.1 gives the full distributions. Similar differences in actions and repeated reads also appear in the students evaluation trajectories. On both benchmarks, H5-trained 124B students take fewer actions and repeat fewer file reads on average than H0-trained students. Appendix F.2 reports the comparison. Most collection gains come from mixed histories. Table 21 in Appendix breaks down the gains in Table 4 by history type. Stable-solved issues show no difference in resolved trajectories between H0 and H5. Although mixed histories account for only 51 of the 300 collection issues, they contribute 13 of H5s 16 additional resolved trajectories and five of its six additional solved issues. Never-solved histories account for the remaining three trajectories and one issue. The gains are therefore concentrated on issues whose prior 8 SWE-Trail attempts include both successes and failures. This is consistent with Section 2.2, where such histories reveal decision points that may benefit from additional collection effort.

sections.title: 4.5 How the Collection Mechanism Changes
sections.content: History leads to more comparisons. Figure 3 compares H0 and H5 across the stages of collection. With history, candidate sampling occurs in 1,147 of 1,500 rollouts, compared with 664 under H0. Both suffixes are executed in 968 rollouts under H5 and 560 under H0. Panel shows that candidate sampling increases by 29.8 percentage points on mixed histories and 35.4 on never-solved histories, compared with 17.3 on stable-solved histories. This pattern is consistent with using disagreements and repeated failures to identify where more collection effort may be useful. More comparisons, similar selection rates. Panel shows similar candidate diversity under H0 and H5, with at least two distinct actions in about 90% of candidate-sampling cases. The increase in comparisons therefore comes mainly from candidate sampling occurring more often. Panel shows better local progress on one route in 40.7% of H5 rollouts and 28.7% of H0 rollouts. Yet Panel shows similar alternative-selection rates among completed comparisons, at 37.4% and 39.0%, respectively. Together, Panels and show that H5 more often reaches comparisons with clear progress, while the rate of selecting the alternative remains similar. Figure 3. History leads to more comparisons. Conditional on candidate sampling, candidate diversity remains similar, as does the alternative-selection rate. Table 22 in Appendix gives the full funnel and counts by history type.

sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Three lines of work relate to SWE-Trail. Appendix gives the extended discussion. Test-time search and selection. Search methods spend extra compute to solve the current issue. Some sample several independent rollouts and select among them using tests or model judgments (Ehrlich et al., 2025). Others reuse earlier prefixes or summaries of prior attempts to guide later rollouts on the same issue (Ding and Zhang, 2026; Kim et al., 2026). Tree search explores alternatives within growing execution tree during the current solve (Antoniades et al., 2025; Kocsis and Szepesvári, 2006; Zhou et al., 2024). Instead, SWE-Trail uses prior attempts on the same issue to guide where additional collection effort is spent during trajectory generation. The coding agent proposes actions from its current context, SWE-Trail briefly compares them from the same checkpoint, and the selected route becomes the training trajectory. Trajectory generation and curation. Methods for constructing training data generate more tasks and trajectories or increase trajectory diversity through adaptive synthesis (Chen et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025). Others select resolved trajectories or modify completed trajectories through filtering and process-level editing (Han et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026a; Pan et al., 2025; Tao et al., 2026). Recent work also evolves curation rules using downstream failures (Wang et al., 2026a). Instead, SWE-Trail uses prior attempts on the same issue to guide where additional collection effort is spent during trajectory generation. These comparisons collect new execution evidence rather than only selecting or modifying completed trajectories. Post-hoc selection can still follow, as Section 4.3 shows. Experience-guided agents. Agents use reflections, distilled insights, workflows, and skills to guide later actions (Li et al., 2026a; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025b; Zhao et al., 2024). For coding tasks, this experience can come from earlier repair trajectories, human debugging records, or the ongoing attempt (Chen et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Hayashi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b). These methods use experience to guide 9 SWE-Trail the agents reasoning or actions. Instead, SWE-Trail uses history to guide where additional collection effort is spent. The coding agent proposes actions from its ordinary context without receiving that history.

sections.title: 6 Discussion and Limitations
sections.content: What the results show. The experiments separate collection success from downstream training value. H0 resolves more trajectories than independent sampling but brings little gain on Multilingual, while adding history in H5 produces larger student gains. Randomizing either where additional collection effort is spent or which executed route continues lowers mean resolution relative to H5. The gains also appear with Qwen3-14B-Base. These results support using history as collector-side signal for improving the training value of new trajectories, rather than as advice shown to the coding agent. Limitations and future work. Our experiments use two student models but one collection model and one agent scaffold. Future work could test other collection models and scaffolds. Our current setting also keeps history fixed during each collection round and uses the same collection budget for every issue. Future work could update history across rounds and allocate effort differently across issues. The exploratory replay audit in Appendix G.1 also motivates testing more diverse candidate proposals. Extending SWE-Trail beyond coding would require environments that support state restoration and feedback for comparing alternatives. Web navigation is one possible direction.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: Our results point to broader lesson: prior attempts are useful not only for what they contain, but also for guiding where new collection effort should be spent. SWE-Trail operationalizes this idea by compiling prior attempts into rules that determine when additional collection effort may be useful during new rollout. The coding agent proposes actions without seeing the history, while the collector briefly executes candidates from the same checkpoint and uses the resulting evidence to choose which route to continue. With the training setup fixed, SWE-Trail improves the 124B students mean resolution over independent sampling by 2.33 percentage points on SWE-bench Multilingual and 1.60 points on SWE-bench Pro. The gains also appear with Qwen3-14B-Base. The H0 comparison shows that collection success alone does not explain the downstream gains. Randomizing either where additional collection effort is spent or which executed route continues lowers mean resolution relative to H5. Together, these results show that prior attempts can improve the training value of new trajectories by guiding collection without being shown to the coding agent as advice. 10 SWE-Trail

sections.content: C.1 Collection Issues and Prior Attempts The main experiments use 300 repository-level issues from SWE-rebench V2 (Badertdinov et al., 2026), with one issue per repository. Each collection condition produces five trajectories per issue. SeedBank provides the five independently sampled attempts used as history by H5. H10 adds five more eligible attempts to the same five, giving ten prior attempts per issue. We define three history types from the outcomes of the five SeedBank attempts before the main collection begins. The stable-solved group contains 37 issues for which all five attempts succeed. The mixed group contains 51 issues with both successful and failed attempts. The never-solved group contains 212 issues for which all five attempts fail. These labels describe the observed SeedBank outcomes and are separate from how the compiler interprets each history. Appendix F.5 reports the compiler classes. Collection runs in an offline sandbox with no network access and no repository commit history. The coding agent sees the working tree at the issue commit but cannot access later commits. The reference patch, fixing commit, and externally published solutions are also unavailable. The read-only repository checks in Section 3.1 follow the same restrictions. Any information already encoded in the model weights is shared across conditions, since all collection conditions use the same model on the same issue set. 24 SWE-Trail C.2 Evaluation Benchmarks and Overlap Audit We evaluate on SWE-bench Multilingual and SWE-bench Pro. SWE-bench Multilingual, released with SWE-smith (Yang et al., 2025), contains 300 issues across nine languages: C, C++, Go, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, PHP, Ruby, and Rust. Appendix E.3 reports results by language. SWE-bench Pro (Deng et al., 2025) contains longer-horizon repository issues whose reference patches typically span multiple files. We use its public split of 731 tasks. Both benchmarks use the evaluation protocol in Appendix D.2. We verify that the collection and evaluation sets do not share issues or repositories. Exact instance IDs and canonical lowercase owner/repository names are compared across the sets. The 300 Multilingual tasks span 41 repositories, and the 731 SWE-Pro tasks span 437 repositories. Neither benchmark shares an issue or repository with the collection pool. C.3 Experimental Conditions The conditions separate three ways of using existing trajectories. The three curation conditions are controlled adaptations rather than full reproductions of the original methods. They modify the same completed SeedBank trajectories without collecting new interactions. SWE-Exp uses prior attempts to create information that is shown to the coding agent during new rollout. SWE-Trail instead keeps prior attempts private to the collector and uses them to guide where additional collection effort is spent. Our SWE-Gym adaptation (Pan et al., 2025) conditions each record on its outcome. Successful records receive the outcome annotation while preserving their original messages and actions. Unresolved records remain unchanged. The adaptation does not apply condition-specific loss mask. Our SWE-Lego adaptation (Tao et al., 2026) applies deterministic tool-error masking to successful records. It masks only assistant turns whose tool result indicates strict tool misuse, including invalid arguments, missing paths, permission errors, or shell syntax errors. Failed tests and bug reproduction output remain trainable. Unresolved records remain unchanged. Our SWE-TRACE adaptation (Han et al., 2026) removes noncritical messages from successful records. It retains interactions involving patch-modified files, validation, final repository inspection, and the final answer. Repeated non-mutating observations are deduplicated. Messages are removed rather than lossmasked. Unresolved records remain unchanged. Our SWE-Exp adaptation (Chen et al., 2025) compiles the same five prior attempts into an experience message. The coding agent receives this message while generating the new trajectory, and the message remains in the exported training record. The SWE-Trail conditions keep prior attempts outside the coding agents context. H0 runs the same collection pipeline without history. H5 uses five prior attempts, while H10 uses ten. Random detection replaces the history-guided comparison location with random eligible state while leaving the remaining collection procedure unchanged. Random retention keeps H5s history-guided comparison location but randomly chooses which executed route continues. sections.title: I Detailed Related Work
sections.content: Section 5 groups the closest work into search and selection, trajectory construction and curation, and experience-guided agents. Here we give broader comparison centered on two questions: who reads prior attempts, and how those attempts affect later computation. Table 28 summarizes the main interfaces. Table 28. How prior attempts are reused. The main distinction is whether history enters the coding agents context or remains private to an external collection procedure. Use of prior attempts Consumer Effect on later computation Primary goal Retrieved reflection or memory Distilled skill or workflow Inference-time replay or refinement History-guided tion (ours) collecCoding agent Coding agent or workflow Search harness and coding agent Collector Adds previous feedback or experience to the visible context Supplies reusable procedural guidance Reuses prefixes or conditions generation on prior summaries Guides where additional collection effort is spent while history remains outside the agent context Improve the current solve Improve the current solve Improve or select current solution Collect training trajectories I.1 Executable Coding Agents and Trajectory Corpora SWE-bench established executable repository-level repair, while SWE-agent and OpenHands provided widely used coding-agent scaffolds (Jimenez et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2024). SWE-Gym, R2E-Gym, SWE-smith, and Open-SWE-Traces expand the available tasks, environments, rollouts, and languages for training (Ahmad et al., 2026; Jain et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). These efforts increase the supply of coding trajectories. Our focus is different: given several prior attempts on the same issue, we ask how that history can guide the collection of additional trajectories. I.2 Inference-Time Search and Selection common inference-time strategy samples several complete rollouts and selects or combines them using tests, execution outcomes, or model judgments (Ehrlich et al., 2025). Other methods reuse earlier computation more directly. They may restore previous trajectory prefix and continue from an earlier point, or summarize prior attempts and use those summaries to condition later rollouts (Ding and Zhang, 2026; Kim et al., 2026). These methods use additional computation to improve the solution returned for the current issue. Tree-search methods provide another form of adaptive inference. MCTS and related approaches compare alternatives within growing online search tree and allocate computation using value estimates, process 39 SWE-Trail signals, or terminal outcomes (Antoniades et al., 2025; Kocsis and Szepesvári, 2006; Zhou et al., 2024). They can revisit shared prefix and explore alternatives that independent full rollouts may miss. SWE-Trail differs in both source and objective. Its guidance comes from independent attempts collected before the new rollout, and the goal is to collect training trajectories rather than to return the best solution from search tree. It compiles fixed rules before collection and executes at most one comparison during rollout, without recursive tree expansion or value backup. The H0 control in Section 4.1 evaluates this bounded collection procedure without history, rather than full tree-search policy. I.3 Trajectory Construction and Post-Hoc Curation Several methods improve coding-agent training data after trajectories have already been generated. SWEGym and related pipelines retain trajectories based on executable outcomes, while other methods mask flawed tool calls, remove redundant interactions, reconstruct better paths, or use process-level signals to identify more useful supervision (Han et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026a; Pan et al., 2025; Tao et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026b). Data valuation and training-dynamics methods similarly estimate the usefulness of examples that already exist (Ghorbani and Zou, 2019; Koh and Liang, 2017; Paul et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2023). These methods are complementary to SWE-Trail. Post-hoc curation decides which parts of completed data should be retained or emphasized. SWE-Trail instead uses prior attempts while new trajectory is being collected. The comparison can produce new repository evidence that would not exist if the alternative action were never executed. Curation can still be applied afterward. Appendix G.3 evaluates one such combination using verifier-based selection over SeedBank and H5 trajectories. I.4 Training-Time Diversity and Adaptive Curation Recent work treats the training corpus itself as an object to optimize. TDScaling increases trajectory diversity through blueprint-driven synthesis and adaptive task evolution rather than only sampling more trajectories (Chen et al., 2026). Han studies filtering of an existing SWE trajectory pool and reports an interaction between data quality, quantity, and model scale (Han, 2026). CurateEvo represents curation as executable code and updates the curation procedure from downstream failures to construct SFT, RL, and memory data from fixed raw corpus (Wang et al., 2026a). SWE-Trail shares the goal of improving the training distribution but acts at different stage. It changes how new trajectories are collected. Earlier attempts on the same issue guide where additional collection effort is spent, while the coding agent generates the candidate actions without receiving that history. I.5 Experience-Guided Agents Another line of work converts previous interaction into information that helps an agent act later. Reflexion and ExpeL store feedback or reusable experience across attempts (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024). Agent Workflow Memory, CODESKILL, Socratic-SWE, and ProPlay derive workflows, skills, or procedural knowledge from previous executions (Li et al., 2026a; Ma et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2025b; Xiao et al., 2026a). For software repositories, experience may come from earlier repair trajectories, human debugging records, or trajectories produced during the current solve (Chen et al., 2025; Hayashi et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2024; Mu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Xia et al., 2025). Other systems recombine agents or revise failed paths during inference (Ehrlich et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025). The common pattern is that distilled experience changes the coding agents visible context, workflow, or behavior. SWE-Trail keeps that information outside the coding agent. History guides the collector in deciding where additional collection effort may be useful, while the coding agent proposes its next actions from the ordinary context. This separation is central to our training-data setting because the exported trajectory does not depend on history being available to the student at test time. 40 SWE-Trail I.6 Adaptive Acquisition and Harness Optimization The broader idea of allocating computation using previous observations appears in active learning and experimental design, which choose informative examples or experiments (Foster et al., 2021; Kirsch et al., 2019; Sener and Savarese, 2018). Intrinsic-motivation methods similarly direct interaction toward novel or prediction-reducing states (Bellemare et al., 2016; Pathak et al., 2017). For LLM agents, direction-informed gating learns from counterfactual exploration whether state feature indicates that extra rollouts will help or hurt (Li et al., 2026b), and paired rollouts can estimate the value of asking clarification question before acting (Huang et al., 2026). Agent self-improvement and harness-optimization methods adapt prompts, workflows, tools, or control procedures from execution feedback (Lin et al., 2026; Madaan et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2026; Robeyns et al., 2025; Xi et al., 2024). SWE-Trail applies narrower form of adaptive allocation within one issue. The history of that issue is compiled before the new collection round, and the resulting rules remain fixed during the rollout. They guide where additional collection effort is spent and how executed alternatives are compared, without changing the coding-agent prompt, tools, or model weights. Recent results show that simple search can remain strong baseline (Gideoni et al., 2026). We compare against independent sampling, history-free version of the same collection pipeline, randomized controls, and verifier-based selection in Section 4.1.
